one_liner: Fails the quality test (its best days look to be behind it), so price does not matter.

profile.what: PACCAR designs and builds premium trucks under the Kenworth, Peterbilt and DAF names, sells replacement parts, and finances trucks for its customers.
profile.money: Truck sales rise and fall with freight demand. The parts business and the finance arm earn steadier profits and carry most of the debt on the balance sheet.
profile.valued: PACCAR is valued on P/E across the truck cycle. Investors watch truck orders, parts growth and credit losses in the finance arm.

summary.sentence: A conservatively run premium truck maker in the down leg of its cycle.
strengths: Free cash flow has risen through the downturn.
Profitable in every year of the record.
risks: Revenue and earnings have fallen for two years.
Gross margin is thin and cyclical.
Truck demand follows the freight cycle.

meaning.what_it_does: Makes heavy and medium trucks under the Kenworth, Peterbilt and DAF brands, and runs a parts business and a finance arm for its customers.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Truck sales through independent dealers, high-margin replacement parts, and interest on truck loans and leases.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Premium brands hold their resale value, and the parts business earns steadily through the cycle.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: A deep freight downturn cuts truck orders, or the shift to new engine technology goes badly.

moat.summary: Premium brands and a loyal dealer network, in an industry where a few makers compete hard on price in downturns.

industry.summary: Trucks change slowly, but emissions rules and electric drivetrains are forcing heavy investment.

management.summary: Conservatively run for decades: profitable every year, with most debt sitting in the finance arm against truck loans.

financial_health.ratio_gaps: Not available from the data source, so not shown: a ten-year record, inventory and receivables turnover, the quick ratio, goodwill and tangible book value, and maintenance capex split from growth capex. Owner earnings therefore deduct all capex, which is conservative.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow, capex held at depreciation: $4.0B a year: operating cash flow less depreciation and stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). Capex is running at 3.7x depreciation, so most of it is expansion, not upkeep. (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 2–8% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 10%; cost of capital 8.6%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Free cash flow (stock-based pay is not reported separately by the data source, so none is deducted).
